title: Chapter 46 – The Hollow Orchard
html:
[Lin Clan – Lin Jian]

The first Warden is a tree that has learned to walk.

It comes out of the haze at the end of the third row, slowly, with a sound like a very old man clearing his throat, and Jian sees it first as a bend in the light. Then the bend has legs. Four, thick as a man's waist, knotted and gray, with roots for feet that sink into the moss at each step and draw out again with a small wet pop. A trunk, shaped roughly like a body. Two long branching arms, a head without a face, and in the hollow where a face should be, a pale green lamp.

It is the size of a haystack. It is not hurried. It stops six paces from him, and the lamp in its head tilts, with the slow attention of a thing that has been alone for a very long time.

Stand still, says Pebble.

"I am standing."

Stand stiller.

Jian stands stiller. His heart is hammering. He has one hand under his robe on the needle roll, and he has already counted the Warden's joints, and the two seams between trunk and limb where bark gives way to something paler, and found them thick. This is not a rogue with a hole under the arm. A needle would go into that wood the way a pin goes into a door.

He has not been so afraid since the cave. He has only one defense against it, and he uses it: he counts. Eleven paces to the nearest bed. Fourteen to the place where the moss ends. Two breaths, he judges, before that bulk can close the distance, and he is a seventh-stage with a cracked rib and four needles that cannot pierce wood. It is a bad sum. He does it twice, and it is no better.

Be still, Pebble says again, and slides from his collar down his sleeve to the moss.

She walks toward the Warden.

She is a small pale thing in an enormous green hall, a loaf-sized creature with a scaled back and a tail like a rope, and she walks the way she has always walked, with her nose down and her round body swaying, as if nothing in the world could be more important than the smell of the ground. She stops at the Warden's foot. She sits up on her hind legs, and lifts both small hands, and makes a sound.

It is not a word. It is a long soft rolling trill, rising and falling, the kind of sound a mother makes to a child in the dark. Jian feels it in the bond as a wave of warmth, and under the warmth, something very much like homesickness.

The green lamp flares.

The Warden bends its whole vast body, creaking, like a tree in a storm, and lowers its head until the pale light of its face is a hand's breadth from the pangolin's nose. For a long moment they regard each other. Then one huge branching hand reaches down, so slowly that the moss does not stir, and touches the tip of her tail with a single twig.

It knows me, says Pebble, in a voice that shakes. It remembers my mother.

* * *

The Wardens are not alive. Jian understands that after a quarter of an hour, when they have gathered round the clearing in a loose, respectful ring, eleven of them, and he has had time to look.

They are puppets. They are wood and stone, bound with roots, wakened with Qi and given a task. He sees the thread of it, with Pebble's help, a faint gold line running from each Warden's chest down into the moss, to something very deep. It is the formation. It is old and thin and half dead. The Wardens that are left hold it together, he thinks, the way eleven men hold the corners of a very old, very heavy cloth.

Low, he thinks, and then, by habit, he lays the numbers out. Qi Refining, third, fourth, fifth stage. Ten of them. And the last.

The last stands apart, at the foot of a flight of broad stone steps, taller than the others and darker, built of black basalt with a hide of green moss. It has a huge round shield on one arm, a doorway-sized slab of gray granite. The lamp in its head is not green, but amber. It has not moved since he arrived. It has not taken its eyes off him.

That is the gate one, says Pebble. That is the big one. It is not like the others. It does not like you.

Why?

You smell of the cold place. She turns her head, and her small dark eyes are troubled. The place where the bad people live. You smell of their blood. A little. On your hands.

He looks down. In the green light, on the knuckles of his right hand, there is a faint dried rust-colored smear. It is Mei Ru's blood, from the binding. He wipes it on his robe. It does not come off.

Tell it, he says slowly, that I am a friend of yours.

I did. She sounds rueful. It says you are a friend of mine. It does not say you are a friend of its.

"That," says Jian aloud, to the amber lamp, "is fair."

* * *

The woman is still unconscious. He has dragged her, with some difficulty, to the foot of the nearest bed, and laid her against a boulder with her good arm under her head, and she looks, in the soft light, much younger than she did in the quarry. Her face is slack. Her mouth is open a little. A pale green moth has settled on her forehead.

She wakes at the second hour.

He is sitting cross-legged, a few paces off, with a needle between his fingers and the Veil drawn close, watching her breathe. She opens her eyes. She looks at the glowing ceiling for a long time, without any expression. Then she turns her head.

"Ah," says Mei Ru, in a hoarse small voice. "So it was not a dream."

"No."

"I am not dead."

"No."

"That is a great pity. I had made all the arrangements." She wets her cracked lips. "Where is this?"

"I don't know."

"You are lying. Not about that." Her gaze moves over him, over the needle in his hand, over the thread of Qi. "You are lying about whether you will kill me. You have been trying to decide for two hours. I can feel it. You are a child who has never learned how to put a thing down."

He does not answer. The moth lifts from her forehead and drifts away into the haze.

"I used the Blood Fox," she says, after a time. "It burns the blood. I should be a husk. Instead I have a pulse." She turns her head, slowly, and looks at her own arm. At the black binding, and the grayish scab under it, and the fresh pink skin at its edges. "You put something on this."

"A pill."

"A Blood Seal. I know the smell. It is Tally's." Her eyes close. "You took it from his satchel. And then you gave it to me."

"It was in my pocket."

"That is not an answer."

"No," says Jian. "It isn't."

She laughs, very softly, without opening her eyes. It has no edge. It is the laugh of a woman too tired to hold on to anything.

"Do you know what the funny thing is?" she says. "If it had been me. If I had found you. I would not have been so stupid." A pause. "Mu always said that kindness was a tool for the weak. He is, I think, a very wise man. And I find I do not care."

"Be quiet. The Warden will hear you."

"The what?"

Behind her, in the gloom, the amber lamp turns, and the great black shape of the gate-Warden takes a single slow step forward.

Mei Ru opens her eyes.

She screams.

* * *

It is not a cry of fear. It is a sound of pure animal outrage, ripped out of her throat, and she is on her knees before Jian can move, with her good hand clawing at the empty air for a chain that is not there. The amber lamp blazes. The granite shield comes up.

No, says Pebble. No, no, no.

The Warden does not strike. It lifts one vast black arm, and from the knuckles, thin as wire, a hundred pale roots whip out across the moss, faster than anything that size has a right to move. They wrap Mei Ru's ankles. They wrap her wrists. They climb her body in a single coiling spasm, and a root as thick as his arm closes across her mouth.

She falls. She does not struggle. Her eyes are wide above the green knot, and they are fixed on his.

"Stop," says Jian. He is on his feet. He does not remember rising. "Pebble. Tell it to stop."

It is not killing her. Pebble is a pale streak across the moss, up the Warden's leg, onto its shoulder, trilling. It says, she cannot go loose. It says, she is a thorn. It says, a thorn must be held until the gardener decides.

"Who is the gardener?"

I do not know. The small voice is full of doubt. I think... it means you.

Jian stares. The amber lamp is steady. It is not hostile, not any longer. It is waiting. It has put the question to him, in the only language it has, and it will hold the roots, as it has held its station for however many hundreds of years, until it is answered.

I am ten years old, he thinks, with a kind of weary wonder. I have been asked to be a gardener by a stone.

"Hold her," he says. "Do not hurt her. Not yet."

The roots loosen a fraction. Mei Ru draws a ragged breath around the knot in her mouth. Her eyes are very bright.

"Not yet," Jian says again, more quietly. "I haven't decided."

* * *

The heart of the Orchard is a quarter of a mile farther in.

He walks there with Pebble on his shoulder and two small Wardens lumbering at his heels, because they will not let him go alone. They are not very large, as Wardens go. They have the bodies of old stumps and the long thin arms of the willow. The little one on the left drags one root, as if lame. He thinks of it, for no good reason, as Limp.

They pass the herb beds, row on row. He counts as he goes, because he cannot help it. Thirty-one species, the panel said. He knows four. Red-thread root, for blood. Sunfern, for fever. A pale blue flower that Hu once pressed in a book and called mourner's cup, good for pain. And a tall tangle of silver-gray leaves, with small white berries like pearls, that makes his heart skip. Heartroot. The name is in Tally's slip, on a recipe for a pill he has never seen.

A herb like that is worth a sack of stones, he thinks. And there are forty of them. Fifty.

Then the beds end, and he comes out into the open, and stops.

Before him is a pool.

It is not large. A circular basin of white stone, forty paces across, sunk into the moss and rimmed with a low carved wall. The water in it is perfectly still, and it is lit: a deep, dusky, shimmering green, like a gem held up to the sun. A thin, cold mist rises from the surface. It smells of rain, and iron, and a faint sweetness, like a flower he cannot name. When he draws it into his lungs it goes down like cool silk, and where it touches his channels he feels them open.

```
[ARK-7 — SCAN]
Object: Spirit-vein reservoir (miniature; sealed).
Qi content: ~4,200 units (clan-scale: see note).
Regeneration: ~0.4% of capacity per day.
Output at present: 40 low-grade stones/season (est.),
plus one batch of herbs.
Note: Reservoir is a remnant. It cannot sustain a sect.
It could sustain a village.
```

A village, Jian thinks. Forty stones a season, and a harvest of herbs that Hu could turn into a hundred more. It is not a fortune. It is the difference between a clan that is slowly strangled and one that is merely poor.

He thinks of Wenjun's ledger, the three hundred stones of tribute, the forty short. He thinks of Mao's daughter, and the pension that was never earned. He thinks that the thing he has found is exactly the size of the thing the hill needs, and that this is not how luck works, and that someone, perhaps a long time ago, did the same sum.

A village, he thinks again. Or a clan. A clan of four hundred, on a dying hill, with its vein at three parts in a hundred.

He sits down at the edge of the pool, heavily, and puts his face in his hands.

* * *

On the far side of the basin, on a low raised terrace of black stone, a circular plate has been set flush into the floor.

It is twice the width of a man's outstretched arms. It is made of some dark, dull metal that gives back no reflection, and its face is carved with a lattice of fine lines, so fine and so exact that his eye refuses to rest on them. It is a lock. He knows it before he is within ten paces. It has the same shape, the same intent, as the one at the fortieth step of the Gate Trial, the one he has stared at for two years, without being able to open.

A cousin, he thinks. Not the same. A younger sister.

In the center of the plate, a flat gray disc the size of his palm lies in a shallow hollow, as if it had been placed there to keep a place warm.

And beside it, tied with a faded blue cord and wrapped in oiled silk, is a half roll of old paper.

He climbs the three black steps. Behind him, the Wardens stop at the foot of the terrace, and do not follow. Limp makes a small anxious creaking sound and lowers its head.

Jian kneels. He looks at the disc. He does not touch it.

It is the color of old iron. It is warm. When he holds his hand a finger's breadth from its surface, he feels a faint steady pulse, a heartbeat, slow and strong. It is not a piece of the lock. It is a thing that has been put here, deliberately, by a hand that knew what it was.

It feels like the thing at the root of the interface itself, he thinks. The same warmth. The same patience.

A second piece. There was a first, and there will be more.

The interface has been silent for an hour. He feels it now, a shift at the back of his mind, as a sleeper feels a hand on the blanket.

```
[ARK-7 — NOTICE]
Component detected: FRAGMENT 2 of ?.
Compatibility: confirmed. Interface resonance: strong.
Integration will consume the fragment.
Integration will NOT be reversible.
Proceed? [Y/N]
```

His hand is not quite steady. He has always known there would be a second piece. Every system, he thinks, has an end that it points toward; the interface has always been a little too clever, a little too accommodating, a little too ready with its small flat sentences. It is the sort of thing that wants to be whole. And he has never once asked what it wants it for.

Everything has a cost.

He has paid for the first fragment in two years of silence, in a body that would not stop. He is not sure what this one will take. He can feel it humming under his hand like an animal, like a thing that has waited a very long time, and is not impatient, and is not at all unaware that he is afraid.

If I do not, he thinks, the Blood Shadow will. Mu is looking for a door in this hill. He will find it. And he will lift this disc with a bloody hand, and the interface will go to him.

It will not. It is a small, firm, unfamiliar thought, and it is his own. It is mine.

He says, aloud, in a voice that sounds odd in the green hush: "Yes."

* * *

It does not hurt, which is the worst part.

He has braced for pain. He has been braced for pain all his life. But the disc rises from its hollow like a drop of water drawn up a thread, and turns over once in the air, and settles against his palm. It is warm as a living hand. It is very light. And then it is not there, and something very small and very cold slides down the inside of his arm and into his chest, and spreads.

He lies on the black stone with his eyes open, looking up at the pale ceiling, and the silver veins of the roof are moving. They are running together, branching, rivering, forming a pattern, a vast soft map of lines, and he sees that it is the same pattern, the same design, as the lattice on the plate beneath him. They are the same thing. They have always been the same thing. The plate is the key, and the roof is the lock, and the Orchard is the keyhole.

I do not understand it.

```
[ARK-7]
Not yet.
```

Two words, in the plain white type it always uses. It is the first time the interface has ever declined to explain itself.

Then the panel is gone, and the ceiling is stone again, and he is lying on a floor, shaking, with his heart going like a hammer and Pebble sitting on his chest, patting his chin with both small hands in a distinct and anxious rhythm.

You were gone, she says. You were gone a long time. I could not feel you. I shouted.

"How long?"

The length of a very long breath. Then three more.

He pushes himself up on his elbows. His whole body feels rinsed. The ache in his rib is gone. The weight in his head has lifted, and the green haze of the Orchard air, which a moment ago was a presence, has become merely a thing he can see. He breathes, and the Qi that comes in is thick and sweet and no longer too much.

```
[ARK-7 — SYSTEM]
Fragment 2: integrated.
Creation Energy: +25. Current CE: 195.
Level 3 prerequisites: CE 200 [195/200], QR8 [QR7 early].
New: Orchard Bell registered (location: heart plate, north).
New: Interface note storage (limited).
Reminder: Everything has a cost.
```

Reminder. He lets out a small, breathless laugh that has no humor in it at all. "Yes. I know."

* * *

The scroll is where he left it.

He had forgotten it, in the rush of the other thing. It lies in its oiled silk at the edge of the plate, under the faded blue cord. When he touches it, the silk comes away in a soft crumble, and underneath, the paper is yellow as old teeth, and brittle, and torn clean across the middle. A half scroll. The edge is ragged, as though somebody, long ago, had halved it with a knife, and taken the other half away.

The characters are tiny and cramped, written in a hand he does not know. The title, in the top right corner, is half lost.

Five Seasons Seed Canon. Part One: the Seed.

He reads the first line, and his mouth goes dry.

That which grows in five elements shall be neither fire nor water, neither wood nor stone nor iron, but the quiet between them: the soil from which all five rise, and to which all five return.

Five-element root. The words go through him like a bell. It is a method for a five-element root. It is not a patched, borrowed manual for a pseudo-root, a stray scrap that mentions the possibility in a footnote. It is a Canon, a founding text, written by someone who had understood what the five dim crystals in his dantian might be for. It tells him, in cramped, impatient characters, how to draw the elements down into a single seed of Qi, and plant it, and let it root.

He reads it all. It takes a long time. The paper is thin and the writing is dense, and at the end of the page the text stops, in the middle of a sentence, at the ragged edge of the tear.

...and in the second season the seed shall put forth a shoot, which shall seek out the

That is all. Half a method. A Seed with no Sprout. He holds it in both hands, and the light of the pool moves across it in slow green ripples, and for the first time in his two lives he feels something that is not caution, and not calculation, and not fear.

It is hope. It is entirely unreasonable. It makes his hands shake.

The other half, he thinks. Someone has the other half.

* * *

He is turning back toward the pool when Pebble stiffens on his shoulder.

Bell, she says.

"What?"

Bell. Bell. Mother's bell. She is pointing, with one small trembling claw, at the far edge of the terrace, where the black stone gives way to a thicket of reeds. There. I know it. I know the smell. It rang when I was small. It rang and the door opened and the light came in, and Mother went out and she did not come back.

He crosses the terrace. In the reeds, half sunk in the moss, hangs a small bronze bell on a bracket of weathered iron. It is no larger than a man's two fists. It is green with age. The clapper is a single round stone the size of a pebble.

```
[ARK-7 — NOTICE]
Object: Orchard Bell (registered).
Function: Opens a temporary seam to the Green Pine hillside.
Two-way. Exit point: quarry, east wall.
Requires: one clear note, struck by a living hand.
Cooldown: 1 hour. Warning: the seam is visible from outside.
```

An exit, he thinks. And an entrance.

He stands there a long time, with his hand an inch from the green metal. The Orchard hums around him, soft and vast and patient. Behind him, at the edge of the glowing pool, eleven Wardens stand in a loose silent ring, and the amber lamp of the gate keeper has turned toward him, like a lamp turned toward a door.

Dawn, he thinks. Mother said dawn.

He does not know how long he has been in here. The light does not change. He does not know whether it is an hour or a night. But he knows that there is a woman standing in a cold quarry with a knife in her hand and her eyes on a place in the air that is no longer there, and that he has promised her everything.

He takes a breath. He has a strange, quiet, unprecedented feeling, that he is no longer a boy who has been lent a door. He has been handed a key. It is not a gift. It is a debt.

It will have to be paid, he thinks. By someone.

He strikes the bell.

The note is clear, and long, and sweet. It goes out over the Orchard in a ring of silver sound, across the glowing pool, along the beds, and up into the stone sky. And, somewhere very far above, through six hundred meters of rock and root and sleeping earth, a hundred green pines begin to hum.
